parsed_answer.content: A deadlock is a specific state in multithreaded programming where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource held by the other. This creates a circular dependency that prevents any of the involved threads from progressing, effectively freezing that portion of the application. Deadlocks occur when four conditions—known as the Coffman conditions—are met simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion (resources cannot be shared), Hold and Wait (a thread holds one resource while requesting another), No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken from a thread), and Circular Wait (a closed chain of threads exists where each holds a resource requested by the next). Detection involves identifying this circular dependency, while prevention requires breaking at least one of these conditions through careful architectural design.

items: Lock Ordering: Always acquire locks in a consistent global order across the entire application to eliminate circular wait.
Timed Locking: Use tryLock(long time, TimeUnit unit) instead of synchronized blocks to allow threads to back off if a resource is unavailable.
ThreadMXBean: Java provides the java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean interface, which can programmatically detect deadlocks by calling findDeadlockedThreads().
Resource Hierarchy: Assign a numeric rank to all resources and mandate that threads must acquire locks in increasing order of rank.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Insight: Never rely solely on ThreadMXBean for production deadlock resolution. While it is excellent for logging, a deadlock is often a symptom of poor lock granularity. If you find yourself needing to detect deadlocks frequently, your locking strategy is likely too coarse-grained; consider using java.util.concurrent locks or non-blocking data structures like ConcurrentHashMap to eliminate the need for manual synchronization entirely.

title: What is a Deadlock? How do you detect and prevent it?
